order.subject: science
order.requests: Students use phones and Chromebooks. The review app should have the vocabulary and the Rossetti poem we read.

notes: Students show their work on calculations

documents.title: Weather Data Practice
documents.directions: Answer each question. Show your work on the calculations.

questions.prompt: Water vapor cools and turns into tiny drops of liquid water. What is this change called?
questions.hint: Think of drops forming on the outside of a cold glass.
questions.why: Condensation is gas turning into liquid. Evaporation goes the other way, precipitation is water falling from clouds, and transpiration is water leaving plants.

miss.why: Evaporation is liquid turning into vapor: the opposite direction.

questions.prompt: Rain, snow, sleet and hail are all kinds of what?
questions.hint: It's the step of the water cycle when water falls from clouds to the ground.
questions.why: Precipitation is any water that falls from clouds: rain, snow, sleet or hail.

questions.prompt: Warm air is less dense than cold air, so warm air tends to rise.
questions.why: Heated air spreads out, so the same amount of air takes more space: it is less dense and rises above cooler air.

questions.hint: The word comes from the Greek “baros”, which means weight.
questions.why: A barometer measures air pressure. A thermometer measures temperature, an anemometer measures wind speed, and a rain gauge measures rainfall.

miss.why: An anemometer spins in the wind: it measures wind speed.

questions.prompt: At 6 a.m. the temperature was −4 °C. By 2 p.m. it was 9 °C. By how many degrees did the temperature rise?
questions.hint: Count up from −4 to 0 first, then from 0 to 9.
questions.why: From −4 up to 0 is 4 degrees, and from 0 up to 9 is 9 more: 4 + 9 = 13 degrees. Or 9 − (−4) = 13.

miss.why: 9 − 4 = 5 treats −4 as if it were 4. Start at −4 and count up to 9.

questions.prompt: A rain gauge collected 12 mm, 0 mm, 7 mm, 5 mm and 6 mm of rain on five days. What was the mean (average) rainfall per day?
questions.hint: Add all five amounts, then divide by the number of days.
questions.why: 12 + 0 + 7 + 5 + 6 = 30 mm, and 30 ÷ 5 days = 6 mm a day. The 0-mm day still counts as a day.

miss.why: 30 ÷ 4 leaves out the day with 0 mm. It was still one of the five days.

questions.prompt: On 20 school days in March, 15 days were cloudy. What fraction of the days were cloudy?
questions.hint: Write cloudy days over all the days, then simplify.
questions.why: 15 cloudy days out of 20 is 15/20, and dividing both by 5 gives 3/4.

miss.why: 1/4 is the share of days that were not cloudy (5 of 20).

questions.prompt: The barometer reading is falling quickly. Which weather is most likely on the way?
questions.hint: Falling pressure means a low-pressure system is coming. What does low pressure bring?
questions.why: Falling air pressure usually means a low-pressure system is arriving, and low pressure brings rising air, clouds and often rain or storms.

questions.prompt: Air temperature drops about 6.5 °C for every 1 km you climb. It is 20 °C at the bottom of a 2 km tall mountain. About what is the temperature at the top?
questions.hint: First find how much colder it gets over 2 km, then subtract that from 20.
questions.why: Over 2 km it gets 2 × 6.5 = 13 °C colder, and 20 − 13 = 7 °C.

miss.why: 20 − 6.5 is the temperature after only 1 km. The mountain is 2 km tall.
It gets colder as you climb, so subtract the 13 degrees.

questions.prompt: Town A had 840 mm of rain this year. Town B had 3/4 as much rain as Town A. How many millimeters of rain did Town B get?
questions.hint: Find 1/4 of 840 first, then 3 of those parts.

miss.why: 210 mm is 1/4 of 840. Town B had 3 of those quarters.

questions.prompt: Explain why a puddle dries up faster on a hot, windy day than on a cool, still day. Use the word evaporation.
questions.answer: Evaporation is liquid water turning into water vapor. On a hot day the water gets more energy, so it evaporates faster, and the wind carries the damp air away so more water can evaporate.
look: names evaporation as liquid to vapor
wind moves the moist air away
questions.why: Heat speeds up evaporation, and wind replaces the damp air over the puddle with drier air.

passages.title: Who Has Seen the Wind?
passages.text:
Who has seen the wind?
Neither I nor you:
But when the leaves hang trembling,
The wind is passing through.

Who has seen the wind?
Neither you nor I:
But when the trees bow down their heads,
The wind is passing by.

questions.prompt: In which layer of the atmosphere does almost all weather happen?
questions.hint: It is the lowest layer, the one we live in.
questions.why: The troposphere is the lowest layer. It holds almost all the water vapor, so clouds and weather form there.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the tool that measures wind speed?
questions.hint: It has little cups that spin in the wind. Its name starts with “anemo”, Greek for wind.
questions.why: An anemometer's cups spin faster when the wind is faster.

choices: From low pressure toward high pressure
From high pressure toward low pressure
From warm water toward cold land
Straight up from the warm ground
questions.hint: Air is pushed from where it is crowded to where it is less crowded.
questions.why: Air moves from higher pressure toward lower pressure, the way air rushes out of a balloon.

questions.prompt: Humidity is the amount of water vapor in the air.
questions.hint: Think of a sticky, muggy summer day.
questions.why: Humidity measures water vapor, the gas form of water, in the air.

questions.prompt: It is 3 °C in the evening. Overnight the temperature falls 8 degrees. What is the temperature in the morning?
questions.hint: Count down 3 degrees to 0, then keep going below zero.
questions.why: 3 − 8 = −5. Falling 3 degrees reaches 0, and 5 more goes to −5 °C.

questions.prompt: What is the boundary where two air masses meet called?
questions.hint: Weather forecasters talk about a cold one and a warm one moving in.
questions.why: A front is the boundary between two air masses; cold fronts and warm fronts bring changes in weather.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of condensation?
choices: A puddle drying up in the hot sun
Snow melting into slush on a road
Water freezing into ice in a tray
Dew forming on cool grass at dawn
questions.hint: Condensation turns a gas into a liquid. Which one makes liquid water appear out of the air?
questions.why: Dew is water vapor from the air condensing on cool grass. Drying is evaporation, melting and freezing are changes between solid and liquid.

questions.prompt: What do we call liquid water turning into water vapor?
questions.hint: It is how a puddle disappears on a sunny day.
questions.why: Evaporation turns liquid water into water vapor, a gas.
